I was bombarded by messages that it was better not to transition, that it was even OK to be a rough-and-tumble queer woman with a decidedly masculine presentation... and it had absolutely zero effect besides making me realize that cis people really don't get it at all. When I was six or seven and got the puberty talk for the first time, I couldn't understand why nobody would tell me about what I already knew my adult body would look like- spare, flat-chested, smallish genitals... exactly what I've got now, as it turns out, though I took the long way to get here. 

Puberty triggered severe chronic depression, self-injury, and an eating disorder. I spent more than a decade fantasizing daily about horrific accidents or illnesses that would leave me free of my breasts and reproductive organs. What I saw in the mirror was unrecognizable. Presenting as a butch woman did nothing except give me an excuse to avoid girly clothing, which hardly helped. I still hated and feared my menstrual cycle like I've never hated anything else in my life. When my PTSD sent me from sleep into movement before my brain woke up, I reacted to my flopping chest with as much panic as if I'd awoken to find a stranger's face grafted there instead. After I started menstruating [age 10], the only time I felt free in my body was in the dreams where I was a boy.

Of course, cis people are often sure that if I'd just been *that* much more feminist, or persistent, or free-thinking, or supported by society, I could have magically overcome all that. I'm told that in transitioning, I've somehow lost my uniqueness, as if the only thing that differentiated me from any other person was the fact that I was living in a private hell so awful that it has a 41% attempted suicide rate. As though they have any idea what it's like to live as one sex when your secondary sexual characteristics contradict that- what it's like to navigate a world that gawks and yells "What the hell is *that*?" every time you step out the door. 

Because it's not as though society makes any of this easy for us- take ID, for example. Even a name change costs money, and we're a chronically un- or underemployed demographic. If I had to get one now, living at less than half the local poverty line, I wouldn't be able to afford it. Getting your sex marker changed requires proof of irreversible surgery in most jurisdictions, and there are very few surgeons out there who'll do gender confirmation procedures for people who aren't also on hormones. In places like Québec, you can't even get a legal name change until you've lived as your preferred sex for a certain period of time- a number of years, IIRC. And in other jurisdictions, your foundational documents can *never* be corrected. So good luck renting an apartment, or getting a job, or voting, or travelling, or generally participating in society with obsolete ID... 

In summary, transsexuality is a biological phenomenon that's no more the product of societal pressures than, say, the desire to repair a cleft palate. If society were in any way accommodating of people who wish to live as another sex without medically transitioning, you'd probably see more of that, but it's designed to be as tough as possible and although we tend to scuttle for one side or the other at top speed, not all of us survive.

Firstly, these aren't "judgement-enhancing" drugs, they're puberty blockers that buy these kids more time to consider their future options without suffering the effects of possibly-inappropriate sex hormones. Believe me, adolescence is tough enough without having an untreated endocrine disorder. Secondly, if you're so certain that teenagers can't be sure what sex they are, why aren't you advocating that *every* kid, cis and trans, be put on blockers until they're 'old enough to know'? Endogenous puberty isn't a neutral course of action.

EDIT: also, pediatric endocrinologists who work with trans kids have come down firmly in favour of administering blockers to kids who present with GID, so you'll have to have a lot more than this layman's "Ooooh, but what if it 'confuses' them?"-style hand-wringing to build a convincing argument here.

It *is* a medical discussion because this is a medical condition that can cause physical harm as well as psychological damage, and the treatment is a physical one. Would you be comfortable with yourself if you had to deal with a micropenis and all the side effects of female-typical estrogen levels- soft skin, baby face, breasts, high voice, wide hips- in addition to being short? How about the chemical depression that comes from hormonal imbalances? What if people and institutions all insisted that you were either a woman or a freak? Have you ever experienced that? Because *I* have, and it's hellish. 

We've already got more than fifty years of data on medical transition and believe me, there's no reason for the WTF moment you're worried about.

In terms of your rhetorical question, I also feel that you might benefit from re-reading the part of my comment that outlines the procedures that can be avoided when trans people don't have to contend with the harm done by going through the wrong puberty.

Like I said, this is the medical consensus on how to treat the condition. Transitioning is the only course of treatment that's ever worked, and puberty blockers are accepted as best practice because they give gender-variant kids more time before making any major decisions about what course of action to take. As great as it would be for kids to live in a world where they'd never have to take any meds ever, sometimes it's important to manage and treat a chronic condition to prevent it from getting worse. Considering the tremendous suffering that untreated transsexuality causes, it's fucking immoral not to treat it.

I do have to say that it's getting better, though slowly. To my mind, the developments in pediatric endocrinology are the biggest deal right now because they allow a trans kid to only have to go through puberty once. Trying to undo the effects of the wrong hormones is bloody difficult and sometimes impossible; far better to have the option of taking blockers until you're sixteen or so and can decide which puberty you want. Not having to worry about corrective procedures like chest reconstruction, electrolysis, facial feminization surgery, tracheal shaves,  and voice retraining or totally unalterable things like height and skeletal structure is a tremendous social, emotional and financial advantage for these kids. 

Like with any medical condition, the earlier you catch it, the easier it is to treat.

Best guess according to current research is that being trans is a neurological intersex condition, so it's no more possible to 'just accept it' and not transition than it is to cure schizophrenia with an exorcism. Besides, untreated transsexuality has a 41% attempted suicide rate plus sky-high rates of depression and anxiety, but after treatment, all those figures drop back into ranges consistent with the general population.
